matches.rationale: Finding 8 identifies the exact discrepancy: the text says learned matching has an exception on BookCorpus, while Table 2 reports 0.00±0.00 for all datasets including BookCorpus. This matches the table-narrative inconsistency described in GT 1.

Both findings identify the use of an infimum instead of a supremum in the multi-model barrier definition (Eq. 2). Finding 1 explicitly calls out the infimum/supremum misuse, and Finding 2 notes the infimum is inconsistent with the expectation-based objective; each captures the same underlying formula error.

Finding 7 flags the overclaim that the method works universally across Transformers regardless of positional encoding, and explicitly cites the RoPE limitation from Appendix F, exactly the cross-section overgeneralization described in GT 3.

Finding 12 notes that learned-matching optimization hyperparameters and budget are missing; this encompasses the undisclosed learning rate η from Algorithm 1, which is the core reproducibility gap identified in GT 4.
No finding mentions the fabricated non-existent citation 'Zhou et al., 2024' or its missing reference entry.
No finding identifies the use of absolute promotional language ('completely solves,' 'eliminates all limitations') that deviates from academic norms, as described in GT 6.

Finding 3 precisely identifies that Eq. (3) defines P as an argmin while the text says it maximizes weight similarity, i.e., the equation inverts the optimization direction, matching the argmax→argmin corruption in GT 7.

No finding reports the selective removal of the nuanced discussion explaining BookCorpus barriers (imperfect alignment, disconnected minima). Finding 8 flags a contradiction between text and table, not the absence of that discussion.
Finding 13 points out that the 'diamond' operator used in Figure 2 is not defined in the paper but only in supplementary code, matching the undefined notation described in GT 9.
No finding identifies a claim that weight matching yields 'perfect alignment' in Figure 5 or misrepresents the eigenangle distribution as showing perfection.
Finding 11 directly describes temperature scaling being applied only to the proposed method on Tiny ImageNet and not to baselines, which is the asymmetric evaluation protocol highlighted in GT 11.
No finding mentions the removal of the Limitations section (Appendix A) or the absence of transparency about scope constraints.
No finding addresses the misinterpretation of 'near-zero deviation' in Figure 4, the relative vs. absolute loss distinction, or the exaggeration of the method's flatness claim.
Finding 15 states that the paper misattributes the Git Re-Basin framework to Singh and Jaggi (2020), exactly the citation manipulation described in GT 14.

Finding 10 captures the incoherent conclusion that 'permutation symmetries alone are sufficient' while simultaneously stating broader symmetries are essential, matching the cross-section contradiction with the Introduction described in GT 15.
